John Moses and Joseph Kirkland (eds.), History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 1 (Chicago and New York: Munsell & Co., 1895). Read here for the town before 1836: the immigration chapter 'From Village to City - 1830 to 1837 - the Balloon Age' at printed pages 78-79 and 87-101, the early taverns and hotels at pages 560-561, the 'Real Estate and Insurance' chapter at pages 541-542, the packing trade at page 389, the fire department at pages 207-208, the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy quoted from Blanchard at page 35, and the Biographical sketches of P. F. W. Peck, Philo Carpenter, John Dean Caton and Alexander N. Fullerton at pages 570-577 and 584; and, for the shore of 1812 (T-0471), the chapter 'The Massacre' at pages 49-50, 54 and 60-61 - the low, discontinuous sand-hills south of Twelfth Street, the scattered cottonwoods on the bank's lower reaches, and the two 'Massacre trees' of Eighteenth Street with Mrs. Kinzie's word that they were saplings in 1812.

transcribes.note: PRINTED AT LENGTH AND NOT MERELY CITED. At pages 34-35 the volume introduces the Kinzie and Clybourn genealogy as 'best told by Rufus Blanchard ... He says:' and sets the whole passage as a block quotation, which is why bk_mose1_019 - Benjamin Hall's 1830 arrival and the town's first tannery - is a reading of Blanchard through Moses and Kirkland and not of Moses and Kirkland. This project does not hold Blanchard and cannot check the transcription. Blanchard in turn credits Benjamin Hall himself for the detail, so the chain to the fact is three deep and the claim says so.
transcribes.work: Rufus Blanchard, Discovery of the Northwest and History of Chicago (Wheaton, Ill.: R. Blanchard & Co., 1881)

what_it_does_not_supply: MOST OF WHAT IT WAS FETCHED FOR. Of the forty-nine lead surnames the Newberry index flagged against this work, thirteen earned a claim, twenty-one appear only outside the pre-1836 window, eight appear early and say nothing usable, one (`black`) is only ever the adjective, four are unresolved because the volume carries a surname one character from the index card's spelling, and two are absent outright. The full row-by-row result is committed at data/research/books/moses_kirkland_v1_lead_surnames.json so the next run does not pay for the search twice.

VOLUME 2, WHICH IS HALF THE WORK. Only volume 1 is read. The Newberry cards do not say which volume they cite, so an absence recorded here may simply be in the other book, and every ABSENT verdict in the lookup file says so on itself.

AN INDEPENDENT VOICE. It is a compilation of 1895 and it names its own authorities on the pages read: Andreas for Garrett's $1,800,000 of auction sales, Bross's History of Chicago page 38 for the earliest deeds, the Story of Chicago page 130 for Caton's election tally, Hurlbut's Chicago Antiquities pages 37-8 for the pre-1830 settler list, S. R. Beggs's West and Northwest page 95 for the Black Hawk alarm, and Rufus Blanchard's Discovery of the Northwest and History of Chicago (1881) quoted at length for the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy. Where the sentence itself credits another work, the claim says so and the citation must go to that work and not to this one.
A SINGLE ADDRESS IN THE MODERN SENSE, and no street numbers. Positions here are corners, lots, blocks, a river bank and a tree.

ANY DATE FINER THAN THE YEAR for two things this project wanted finer: Caton's marriage, which is given as '1835' with the scene date sitting in the middle of it, and the Hubbard-Marsh packing partnership, which is 'later'.

CONSISTENCY WITH ITSELF. Page 89 dates Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings to 1832 while page 570 has Peck's occupied in the fall of 1831; page 207 forms the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company on 7 October 1835 while page 570 has it organised on 20 October 1835. Both readings of each are recorded and neither is adopted.
what_it_supplies: A TRADE CENSUS OF THE WHOLE TOWN, at page 95: the State census taken between 1 September and December 1835 counted 3,297 people, forty-four stores, two book stores, four druggists, two silversmiths and jewellers, two tin and copper manufactories, two printing offices, two breweries, one steam saw-mill, one iron foundry, four storage and forwarding houses, eight taverns, one lottery office, one bank, five churches, seven schools, twenty-two lawyers, fourteen physicians, and a lyceum and reading room. The project had no denominator for its business layer and this is one - for December 1835 and not for July.

A BUILDING WITH FOUR OF THE FIVE FIELDS data/structures/ WANTS, at page 90: John S. C. Hogan's story-and-a-half log storehouse, 45 by 18 feet, at the angle where Lake and South Water streets meet, with the post office partitioned off inside it from 2 November 1832.

TWO RESIDENCES STATED AS SUCH, which is the field the town is thinnest in: Rev. Jeremiah Porter lodging and keeping his study in the second storey of Peck's store from May 1833 (page 571), and John Dean Caton renting the back room and attic of Dr Temple's Temple Building from December 1833, sleeping in the attic and practising law in the back room, and sub-letting desk-room in it to his competitor Spring (page 577).

BUSINESSES GIVEN BY CORNER, LOT OR LANDMARK: Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings at the south-east corners of South Water and Dearborn and of South Water and La Salle (page 89); Peck's two-storey frame store of black walnut brought from Detroit, occupied in the fall of 1831 (page 570); Sylvester Marsh killing beef under an old elm on the open prairie at what became Monroe Street from the winter of 1833-4 (page 389); William Jones's lots 2 and 7 in block 17 fronting Water and Lake (page 542).

OCCUPATIONS AND ARRIVALS for men this project already holds: Philo Carpenter as the town's first druggist, arriving within a month before 19 August 1832; Benjamin Hall as proprietor of the first tannery ever established there, arriving 1830; Dole, Clybourn, the Noble brothers and Gurdon S. Hubbard beginning the slaughtering and packing trade in 1832; the 1833 spring arrivals including Caton, Kimball and Asahel Pierce; and Hubbard's permanent residence dated to 1832 by the compiler's own reason for leaving him off a list.

TWO PRESENCE LISTS: the twenty-two men who signed the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company roll on 7 October 1835 (pages 207-208), and, unread and left for its own ticket, the 'LIST OF ACTUAL SETTLERS AT CHICAGO, PRIOR TO 1830' at pages 78-79, about thirty rows with nativity, year and remarks columns.
ONE STATEMENT ABOUT THE GROUND OF THE SCENE, at page 79: the winter of 1834-5 was open, with little snow, front doors standing open all winter, and cattle living on grass on the river bank.

endings.text: Supply chosen, parcel tallied and set down at the shop. The fort is a working neighbour at the river mouth, with stores to keep and a long winter to keep them through.
Part of the note goes back with you. The fort's service buildings will be here tomorrow, and so will the rest of the list, and so will the snow.

evidence.locator: Kinzie, Wau-Bun, ch. XVII ('The fort was inclosed by high pickets … Large gates opened to the north and south'), describing 1831; Andreas vol. 1, p. 84 ('It had two gates, one on the north and the other on the south side').
evidence.text: Fort Dearborn was enclosed by high pickets with large gates to the north and south; Andreas likewise gives the rebuilt fort two gates, one on the north side and one on the south.

evidence.reasoning: Andreas vol. 1, p. 84 gives the two ends of the occupation and no gap between them; the scene date falls inside it. No strength figure for mid-1835 was found, so the stop names none. The gates are shown shut because the stockade record builds its leaves shut; no source states the hour or the state of the gates on the day.
evidence.text: The fort was re-garrisoned in June 1832 and the troops were permanently withdrawn on 29 December 1836, so on 1 July 1835 the post was held.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, p. 264, quoting Hubbard from Fergus' Historical Series No. 10 ('The store-house and guard-house were on either side of the southern gate; the sutler's store was east of the north gate, and north of the soldiers' barracks').
evidence.text: Gurdon Hubbard, describing the fort in July 1827, wrote that the store-house and guard-house were on either side of the southern gate, and the sutler's store was east of the north gate and north of the soldiers' barracks.

evidence.reasoning: Hubbard names the pair without saying which is which, and the 1830 plan draws two small buildings at the gate without naming them. Hubbard puts the magazine 'about half way between the west end of the guard and block-houses', which only describes a real gap if the guard-house is the western building; that is the structure records' reasoning, set out in docs/RESEARCH/fort_dearborn.md.
evidence.text: The guard-house is placed west of the south gate and the store-house east of it.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, p. 264 (Hubbard, 1827); Wentworth, Fort Dearborn (Fergus' Historical Series No. 16, 1881), the key to the 1855 Hesler photograph ('D is the Sutler's').
evidence.text: The north-east range was the sutler's store: Hubbard names it there in 1827, and the key to Hesler's 1855 photograph letters it 'D is the Sutler's'.

evidence.reasoning: The first sentence is what the word means, not a record of this store's trade. Andreas has a sutler employed at the fort about 1830, five years early, so no keeper is named for the scene date; the structure record says the same.
evidence.text: A sutler was a post's licensed trader, selling what the soldiers' ration did not supply. Who held the sutlership at Chicago on 1 July 1835 is not established, and no stock list for this store was found.

evidence.locator: Chicago Democrat, 28 May 1834, p. 3, col. 4 (claim c006: 'at the [st]ore house of Fort Dearborn', 'amounting probably to 400 pounds per week'); 4 June 1834, p. 3, col. 4 (claim c013: 'the subsistance store house of Fort Dearborn'), both signed L. T. Jamison, Ass't Com. Sub., 26 May 1834. Transcription-mediated reading.
evidence.text: The Army's proposals for fresh beef for the Fort Dearborn garrison required it delivered in quarters at the store house of Fort Dearborn, which the second printing calls the subsistance store house, not more than three times a week nor less than once, amounting probably to 400 pounds per week.

evidence.reasoning: The post was held continuously from June 1832 to December 1836 (Andreas vol. 1, p. 84), and nothing records the store-house changing use. The notices do not say which door, so the stop stands outside and claims no entrance.
evidence.text: The notices are thirteen months older than the scene date; the store-house is carried to 1 July 1835 as the garrison's provision store.

evidence.locator: F. Harrison Jr., Map of the Mouth of Chicago River, approved 24 February 1830, as reproduced in Andreas vol. 1, p. 113: the building lettered 'Shop' south-east of the pickets; Hubbard's account at Andreas vol. 1, p. 264.
evidence.text: The 1830 plan draws a building south-east of the stockade, on the fort's outer ground, and letters it 'Shop'. It names no trade. Hubbard's 1827 account, which names the barn, the wash-houses and the other buildings around it, does not mention it.

evidence.locator: p. 99, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 13364-13371 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)
evidence.text: With no railroads, canals or telegraphs, 'during the long six months of winter the inhabitants, were cut off from the rest of the world'. 'There was nothing coming in, and there was no means of sending anything out of the town. And yet these winter months were, perhaps, the most enjoyable of the entire year.'

evidence.locator: p. 574, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 100186-100192 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)
evidence.text: Jeremiah Porter, 'the pioneer Protestant minister of Chicago', came to Fort Dearborn with troops from Fort Brady and 'preached a sermon in the carpenter's shop of the garrison on the 19th of May, 1833'.

evidence.locator: p. 100, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 13395-13406 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)
evidence.text: Another pastime was wolf-hunting: two parties set out in the morning, one down the lake shore and one along the river, and drove the wolves to the river and out to the lake. 'Wolves were in great plenty all around the town', and the chase 'was as exciting as it was at times full of peril'.

evidence.reasoning: The plan is the shop's only witness and is five years before the scene date; the structure record carries it to 1836 on the garrison's continuity. A post of this size usually kept a smith, but the plate says only 'Shop', so no trade is written.
evidence.text: The shop is carried from the 1830 plan to the 1835 scene; whether it was a smithy, a carpenter's shop or something else is not known.

The supply note, the parcel, the choice of candles or thread, the tally, the delivery to the shop, the readiness count, the two endings and the Accounted for at the Fort keepsake are invented connective narrative, not historical events. No sutler's stock, garrison procedure, soldier, sentry or conversation is attested or shown.

keepsake.text: A fictional supply note, tallied outside Fort Dearborn's store-house and carried to the shop on the outer ground.

opening.text:
JAUNT: FORT DEARBORN ERRAND. A winter morning at the river mouth. The lake is iron grey, the boats have stopped, and 'There was nothing coming in, and there was no means of sending anything out of the town.' Out on the prairie, 'Wolves were in great plenty all around the town'. Inside the pickets, the fort keeps its stores.

You carry a note: choose a small supply at the sutler's, check the parcel against the note at the store-house, and take it out to the fort's shop by the lake.

premise: Carry a small supply request round the fort's everyday service buildings and out to its shop.

stops.narrative: State your errand and go on to the sutler's.
stops.text: The fort's south gate, held by troops since June 1832. Juliette Kinzie, living inside in 1831, wrote of high pickets and large gates north and south. Hubbard put the guard-house and store-house either side of this gate in 1827 without saying which; this model puts the guard-house west. In a frozen season, what is in the stores is all there is until spring.

choices.consequence: Light for short evenings at a workbench.
choices.label: A bundle of candles

choices.consequence: Small, light, and always short somewhere.
choices.label: Thread and a paper of needles

stops.narrative: Choose one supply, or go on without it.
stops.text: East of the north gate stands the sutler's store, the post trader's shop, selling what the ration did not supply. Hubbard placed it here in 1827; an 1855 photograph key still letters it the Sutler's. Its 1835 keeper is not known.

choices.consequence: What the note asked for is in the parcel, and you write it down.
choices.label: Tally the parcel against the note

stops.narrative: Account for the parcel before it leaves the pickets.
stops.text: East of the south gate is the store-house. The Army's 1834 beef notices call it the subsistence store house: fresh beef came in quarters, up to three times a week, probably 400 pounds weekly. Check your parcel against the note.

choices.consequence: The errand is done, and the note goes back folded in your pocket.
choices.label: Set the tallied parcel down at the shop

stops.narrative: Deliver what the note asked for, or carry back what is missing.
stops.text: Outside the pickets toward the lake, the 1830 plan draws a building lettered Shop. No trade is named, so this is a workshop, not a smithy. Perhaps it was this one: Jeremiah Porter, 'the pioneer Protestant minister of Chicago', 'preached a sermon in the carpenter's shop of the garrison on the 19th of May, 1833'. Set the parcel down.
